html:
On 21 March 1960 police opened fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws outside the police station in Sharpeville, a Black township south of Johannesburg. They killed 69 people, many shot in the back as they ran.

The Pan Africanist Congress, led by Robert Sobukwe, had called on Black men to leave their passes at home and present themselves for arrest. The passes, required under the pass laws, controlled where Black South Africans could live and work.

The massacre was a turning point:

  • The government declared a state of emergency and banned the PAC and the African National Congress.
  • Both turned to armed struggle; the ANC formed Umkhonto we Sizwe in 1961, with Nelson Mandela among its leaders.
  • The world turned against apartheid, and the UN Security Council condemned South Africa for the first time.

21 March is now Human Rights Day in South Africa, and the United Nations marks it as the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
sum: On 21 March 1960 police opened fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws outside the police station in Sharpeville, a Black township south of Johannesburg. They killed 69 people, many shot in the back as they ran.
